analysis.one_liner: Restores protections for renters living in foreclosed homes, which had just expired.
analysis.headline: The bill to permanently restore expired tenant protections sat in the House Financial Services Committee and never got a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: A 2009 law gave renters in foreclosed homes the right to stay through their lease, or at least 90 days, after a foreclosure. That law had a built-in expiration date of December 31, 2014, and it expired. This bill would strike that expiration date and bring the protections back, permanently.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters living in homes that get foreclosed. Under the restored law, a tenant with a lease could stay until the lease ends, and any tenant would get at least 90 days' notice before eviction — instead of facing immediate eviction by the new owner.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the sunset provision of the Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act of 2009, making the law's protections permanent rather than temporary [S2, S3].
It restores the 2009 Act, the laws it amended, and its regulations as they stood on December 31, 2014, as if the expiration had never taken effect [S2, S3].
The sponsor and 30 cosponsors introduced the bill in the House in March 2015 [S3, S4].

analysis.who_pays: Lenders that foreclose and investors who buy foreclosed homes, who would have to honor existing leases or give tenants 90 days' notice before eviction, delaying taking possession of the property.

drawbacks.text: The protections add costs for buyers of foreclosed homes, who could not immediately take possession, and critics of the 2009 law argued it complicated sales of foreclosed properties and could depress the price lenders recover at foreclosure — a cost that can show up in credit availability for future borrowers (general knowledge about how the 2009 Act works).
Restoring the law retroactively to December 31, 2014 creates legal uncertainty for transactions completed after the law expired, when buyers took possession under different rules [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to tenants is real and targeted: renters — who did not default on the mortgage — would not be thrown out of their homes because of their landlord's default. The costs fall on a narrower group, foreclosure buyers, and mainly delay rather than prevent them from taking the property. The main design flaw is the awkward retroactive restoration, but the core tradeoff favors tenants.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Financial Services Committee, which never took it up, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Keith Ellison introduced the bill on March 13, 2015, with 30 cosponsors [S3, S4].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services [S5].
No further action was taken — the committee never voted on it, the House never voted on it, and the Congress ended January 3, 2017 [S5].
The 2009 tenant protections had already expired on December 31, 2014, so renters in foreclosed homes were without these federal protections throughout the 114th Congress [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Foreclosing lenders and investors who buy foreclosed homes benefited, because without the law they could evict tenants in foreclosed homes immediately instead of honoring leases or giving 90 days' notice.

for.name: Rep. Keith Ellison
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to permanently restore the expired tenant protections.

against.name: Rep. Jeb Hensarling
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee to which the bill was referred, never scheduled it for consideration, and the bill never advanced. The committee's record for the bill shows only the referral [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 30 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-run Financial Services Committee never acted on it [S4, S5].

industries.industry: Lenders and investors who buy foreclosed homes
industries.note: The restored law would force them to honor existing leases or give tenants 90 days' notice before eviction, delaying their takeover of the property. Their gain under the expired law — immediate eviction of renters who never missed a rent payment — comes at those renters' expense.
Tenants, who are not parties to the defaulted mortgage, would keep their homes through the lease term or receive 90 days' notice.
